sections.html:
A Massachusetts quitclaim deed passes along whatever interest the grantor can lawfully convey. Chapter 183, section 2 of the General Laws says a deed of quitclaim and release is enough to convey all the estate that could lawfully be conveyed by a deed of bargain and sale.

The statute also defines the covenants that go with it. Quitclaim covenants, also called limited covenants, mean the grantor promises the property is free of encumbrances made by the grantor, and will defend the title against claims by, through or under the grantor, but against no one else. That is narrower than a promise about the whole history of the title.

The difference is how far the grantor's promises reach. A quitclaim deed with quitclaim covenants limits the guarantee to the grantor's own acts. Massachusetts also provides a statutory form for a warranty deed with broader warranty covenants.

CovenantWhat the grantor promises under M.G.L. c. 183, section 17
Free of encumbrancesOnly those made by the grantor
Defends title againstClaims by, through or under the grantor
Claims from earlier ownersNot covered

A buyer who accepts a quitclaim deed is relying on the grantor's own acts only, so ask your closing attorney what extra title work makes sense.

sections.h2: What a deed must contain to be recorded
sections.html:
Section 6 of chapter 183 sets two musts for any deed sent in for recording. It has to show the buyer's full name, home and mailing address, and it has to recite the full consideration. Those items can also be endorsed on the deed.

  • Full consideration is the whole price, with no subtraction for mortgages or liens the buyer takes on or that stay on the land.
  • When the deal is not for a set amount of money, the deed describes what was given instead.
  • These recitals become part of the recorded deed.
  • A register of deeds must turn away a deed that leaves them out, even though the deed itself stays valid.

Even a gift between relatives needs a stated consideration. A deed missing these details can be refused at the counter, and that can push back a closing date.

sections.h2: Where a Massachusetts deed is recorded
sections.html:
The county Registry of Deeds is where deeds go, and the state runs two title systems side by side. Recorded land is filed with the registry itself. Registered land sits with the Land Court, in districts housed inside the registries.

Roughly 80 to 90 percent of properties are recorded land. Each filing gets a book and page number and shows up online at masslandrecords.com. Registered land has a Certificate of Title that counts as a Land Court decree, so its deeds are handled on the Land Court side.

Find out which system covers your property before you sign anything. Registry staff can answer in minutes, or you can read the current deed at masslandrecords.com.

The base rate in the statute is $2 for each $500, or fraction, of consideration, and $1.50 in Barnstable County. Chapter 64D, section 1 exempts an instrument given to secure a debt, and any deed where the commonwealth, a city or town, or the United States is a party.

Registries post the amount they actually collect. Norfolk County shows $2.28 for each $500 and any fraction of the consideration stated on the deed, with a worked case: $155,000 of consideration means $706.80. Below $100 of consideration, no excise tax is due.

  • Pay the tax when the deed is recorded.
  • Norfolk wants it on its own attorney's check or bank check.
  • Recording fees go on a second check.

Call the registry for your county's current rate and payment rules before closing day.

Each registry sets its own fees. At Norfolk, a deed costs $156 on recorded land, which includes a $1 mailing cost, and $155 on the Land Court side. A declaration of homestead is $36 and a declaration of trust is $256.

Electronic filings skip the $1 postage and return charge as of July 1, 2025. A document that must go on both the Land Court and registry sides needs one check for each. Because other counties post different schedules, ask the registry that will record your deed for its numbers, and bring the payment types it accepts.

sections.h2: Home inspections and attorneys at closing
sections.html:
Under 760 CMR 74, sellers of certain residential properties may not make an offer depend on the buyer giving up a home inspection, and may not take offers from buyers who have said they plan to waive one. Whether your sale falls under it depends on the property.

A Supreme Judicial Court decision also requires an attorney to take a real part in lender closings. Whatever deed you use, plan on an attorney being involved, and ask yours early which documents they will draft.

sections.h2: Does a quitclaim deed fix title problems?
sections.html:
No. The deed hands over whatever the grantor has, and it cannot repair a defect that is already there. It will not reveal liens, tax takings or probate gaps either, so have an attorney decide what title work is needed.

Attorneys are a normal part of Massachusetts sales, by law and by habit. On some purchase money mortgages for homes of up to four families, the lender's attorney must certify title under M.G.L. c. 93, section 70.

  • Check for unpaid property tax or a recorded tax taking.
  • Work out who has to sign, such as a co-owner or an estate representative.
  • Find out whether the land is recorded or registered, because that decides where the deed is filed.
  • Review the deed form with a Massachusetts attorney.

The grantor signs the deed in front of a notary, and the signed original goes to whoever handles the closing. That person takes it to the registry after the funds move, along with one check for the excise tax and another for the recording fees. The registry stamps the deed with a book and page number once it is accepted.

As the seller, ask for a copy of the recorded deed afterward. If the registry rejects the deed for a missing address or recital, the fix is usually quick, but it can hold up the closing for a day or more.

sections.h2: When a quitclaim deed works for a sale
sections.html:
It works when the grantor holds clear title and the buyer is comfortable with limited covenants and a title search. It is a common instrument for sales and for family transfers.

Selling a one or two family home also means getting a smoke and carbon monoxide alarm certificate of compliance from the local fire department. Call them once a closing date is set. When the owner has died, the deed must be signed by a personal representative who has authority to sell, and a lawyer should confirm the steps before a quitclaim deed is used to move the house out of an estate.

A cash buyer who accepts limited covenants can close quickly on a quitclaim deed, as long as the title search comes back clean.

faqs.q: Is a quitclaim deed valid in Massachusetts?
faqs.a: Yes. Under chapter 183, section 2, a deed of quitclaim and release conveys everything the grantor could lawfully pass by a bargain and sale deed.

faqs.q: What does the grantee information on a deed have to include?
faqs.a: The buyer's full name, home and mailing address, plus the full consideration. A register of deeds may refuse a deed without them.

faqs.q: How is the Massachusetts deeds excise tax figured?
faqs.a: The statute's base is $2 per $500 of consideration, while the Norfolk County Registry collects $2.28 per $500. Ask the registry where you record for today's rate.

faqs.q: Where is a quitclaim deed recorded?
faqs.a: At the county Registry of Deeds, on the recorded land side or the Land Court side depending on how the property is titled. Recorded documents get a book and page number.

faqs.q: Where can I look up my deed online?
faqs.a: At masslandrecords.com, which provides access to registry records from across the state.
